The cells that read the ring-trial data are marked #| rtdata. The outputs on this page come from a local run.
08_recalibrate found, on KSSL and IAEA, that fine-tuning for K is a linear recalibration of the zero-shot predictions, while for clay it re-weights the pooled features. This notebook tests both findings on all 21 instruments, with the corrections that need no training:
The last sections add full fine-tuning and the block-4 ridge of 07_finetune, which both train the network.
Each method is fitted on the training folds of each instrument, with the folds of 07_finetune. The starting model is the unaugmented 80-epoch model for each property. The results of KSSL and IAEA come from the saved results of 07_finetune and 08_recalibrate.

rt = load_ringtrial(rt_path())
groups = pd.Series(near_dup_groups(rt['KSSL']), index=rt['KSSL'].sample_ids)
inst_info = load_instruments()[['cluster', 'manufacturer', 'model', 'accessory']]
props, insts, start = ['potassium_cmolkg', 'clay_perc'], list(rt.keys()), 'snv_ep80'
folds = soil_folds(groups)
preds = []
for p in props:
    m = load_pretrained(f'ossl_{p}_{start}')
    for i in insts:
        X, y, ids = rt_xy(rt[i], p)
        tag = dict(instrument=i, property=p, start='not augmented 80')
        rc = cached(f'recal_{i}_{p}_{start}', lambda: cv_recal(m, X, y, ids, folds))
        p0 = pd.Series(predict(m, X, rt_wns).ravel(), index=ids)
        zs = rc[rc.method == 'bias'].assign(method='zero-shot', pred=lambda d: p0[d.sample_id].values)
        pl = cached(f'plsr_{i}_{p}', lambda: cv_plsr(X, y, ids, groups, folds))
        preds += [d.assign(**tag) for d in (zs, rc, pl)]
methods = ['zero-shot', 'bias', 'slope and bias', 'head refit', 'PLSR']
preds = pd.concat(preds, ignore_index=True).query('method in @methods')
test_eq(preds.instrument.nunique(), 21)
test_eq(preds.groupby(['instrument', 'property', 'method', 'repeat']).size().max(), 69)

text:
Results without training
K: the zero-shot predictions are too spread out on every lab. The slope of the targets on the zero-shot predictions is 0.43 to 0.70 on 19 of the 21 instruments, including all the Bruker HTS-XT instruments of cluster 4 (0.53 to 0.70). The two exceptions are Lesotho and UIUC, where the predictions barely correlate with the targets (r² 0.00 and 0.13). The over-dispersion does not depend on the instrument, so it comes from the model or the soils. The predictions are also too high on 19 instruments, by up to 0.36 on the log1p scale. The largest offsets are on IAEA (0.36), Hokudai (0.32), UIUC (0.30), USP (0.26), UGhent (0.24) and OSU (0.22).
K: a linear correction is not always enough. A slope and bias raises the median R² from 0.17 (bias only) to 0.49, and beats the bias alone on 15 instruments. Refitting the head raises it further, to 0.58. It beats the slope and bias on 8 instruments (Argonne, ETH_vertex, LandCare, Lesotho, OSU, Rothamsted, Scion and Hokudai) and never loses. So the finding of 08_recalibrate that K needs only a linear recalibration holds on KSSL and IAEA, but not on these 8 instruments. There, re-weighting the pooled features adds to the linear correction. The head refit beats PLSR on 16 instruments and loses only on UIUC. PLSR reaches a median R² of only 0.22 for K.
Clay: the linear correction is a bias correction, and the head refit adds most. The slope adds to the bias on only 2 instruments. The bias corrections are large on the HTS-XT instruments of cluster 4: their zero-shot offsets are +2.5 to +8.8 points, like the KSSL bias. Refitting the head raises the median R² from 0.67 to 0.82. It beats the slope and bias on 19 instruments and PLSR on 11, and loses to PLSR only on UIUC. With the head refit, R² is 0.87 to 0.94 on cluster 4, 0.61 to 0.89 on cluster 3 and 0.22 to 0.82 on cluster 2.
UIUC and Lesotho. On both, the zero-shot predictions barely correlate with the targets, for K and for clay (r² 0.00 to 0.26). On UIUC, PLSR does better than any correction of the pretrained model: R² 0.42 for K and 0.58 for clay, against -0.14 and 0.22 for the head refit. The UIUC spectra therefore hold information that the pretrained features miss. On Lesotho every method is poor, and PLSR for clay reaches -0.20, so the spectra themselves seem to hold little information. UIUC is a Thermo Fisher Nicolet, like IAEA and OSU, and Lesotho is a PerkinElmer. Both are in cluster 2.

Fine-tuning
Full fine-tuning and the block-4 ridge of 07_finetune, from the same starting model, on the same folds. The number of epochs is the one chosen for this starting model in 07_finetune, by grouped cross-validation on KSSL:

n_epochs = {p: int(cached(f'epochs_{p}', None)['not augmented 80'].idxmin()) for p in props}
ft_preds = []
for p in props:
    m = load_pretrained(f'ossl_{p}_{start}')
    for i in insts:
        X, y, ids = rt_xy(rt[i], p)
        def run():
            pc, hc = cv_cnn(m, X, y, ids, folds, n_epochs[p])
            hc.to_csv(model_dir()/'finetune'/f'hist_{i}_{p}_{start}.csv')
            return pc
        ft_preds.append(cached(f'cnn_{i}_{p}_{start}', run).assign(instrument=i, property=p, start='not augmented 80'))
ft_preds = pd.concat(ft_preds, ignore_index=True).query("method != 'zero-shot'")
methods_ft = methods[:4] + ['ridge block 4', 'fine-tuned', 'PLSR']
preds_ft = pd.concat([preds, ft_preds], ignore_index=True)
scores_ft = repeat_scores(preds_ft, keys).groupby(keys).mean()

title: All labs
text:
Results of fine-tuning
Fine-tuning has the highest median R² for both properties. For K it reaches 0.63, against 0.58 for the head refit, 0.49 for slope and bias and 0.22 for PLSR. For clay it reaches 0.83, against 0.82 for the head refit and 0.59 for PLSR. It beats PLSR on 17 instruments for K and 16 for clay, and never loses to it.
K: fine-tuning adds a small, consistent gain over the head refit. R² is 0.54 to 0.74 on 19 instruments, 0.48 on UIUC and 0.31 on Lesotho. The median gain over the best correction without training or the block-4 ridge is 0.05 R², and the largest is 0.18, on Woodwell_alpha. Fine-tuning beats the slope and bias on 14 instruments and the head refit on 8 (Agrocares, Hokudai, KSSL, Rothamsted, UGhent, UIUC, UWisc_fine and Woodwell_alpha), and loses to neither. The block-4 ridge is poor for K on most instruments (median 0.25), but does well on three of the instruments where the zero-shot predictions correlate least with the targets: UIUC (0.42), UWisc_fine (0.52) and Lesotho (0.32). On Lesotho, PLSR (0.38) is above fine-tuning (0.31), but the difference is not significant.
Clay: fine-tuning matters where the pretrained features fail. On most instruments, the head refit is as good as fine-tuning, and the median difference is 0.00. The head refit is higher on the HTS-XT instruments of cluster 4, for example KSSL (0.94 against 0.90), MSU (0.93 against 0.90) and LandCare (0.92 against 0.88). KSSL is the only instrument where fine-tuning loses significantly. Fine-tuning beats the head refit on 6 instruments: ETH_alpha_1, ETH_alpha_2, IAEA, Lesotho, UGhent and UIUC. The largest gains are on the four instruments with the lowest zero-shot r² (0.10 to 0.32): UIUC (0.22 to 0.70), Lesotho (0.35 to 0.54), IAEA (0.58 to 0.69) and USP (0.61 to 0.69). The block-4 ridge reaches the R² of fine-tuning on IAEA (0.69) and most of it on UIUC (0.63), but not on Lesotho (0.39) or USP (0.60).
What this suggests. Where the pooled features of the pretrained model already carry the property, a refit of the head is enough, and fine-tuning adds little. Where they do not, as for clay on UIUC, Lesotho, IAEA and USP, the inner layers must change. The scores suggest this but do not test it. The questions on where fine-tuning acts, in the roadmap, would test it.
Limits. All the results use one starting model, the unaugmented 80-epoch model, and about 63 training soils per fold. The number of epochs was chosen by cross-validation on KSSL, so the KSSL result is slightly optimistic. PLSR trained only on the instrument’s soils is a weak baseline: a model trained on OSSL with the instrument’s soils added was not tested. The p-values of the 168 paired tests are not corrected for the number of tests.

title: Where transfer fails
section: The instruments where the pretrained features fail
text:
The instruments where the pretrained features fail
The decomposition of 03_instrument_model, on all 20 instruments. For each instrument, a model with shared parameters turns the KSSL spectrum of each soil into that instrument’s spectrum, with all five effects: gain, baseline, shift, broadening and contrast. shared is the RMS of the mean SNV residual over soils, the part that a model with shared parameters can remove. soil is the RMS of what remains after the mean is removed. none is without any effect, full with all five. The fits take about 2 minutes and are cached:

wn = rt['KSSL'].wavenumbers.astype(float)
full = ('gain', 'baseline', 'shift', 'broaden', 'contrast')
def decompose():
    rows = {}

    d = pd.DataFrame(rows).T.unstack()

In 16_moisture, the amplitude of the Fukushima spectra against their OSSL analogues is 1.19.

title: OSSL to ring trial transfer
text:
WarningWork in progress



Pretraining, the zero-shot experiment, the instrument model, the sensitivity check, the augmentation and fine-tuning on two instruments have run. The other experiments below are still to come.
This project tests whether CNN models of soil mid-infrared (MIR) spectra, trained on the Open Soil Spectral Library (OSSL), transfer to other spectrometers. It uses the ring trial of Safanelli et al. (2023), in which 20 laboratories scanned the same 70 soils, each with its own instrument and procedure. A Shimadzu instrument in Japan (Hokudai) also scanned 59 of the soils. The targets are organic carbon, clay, pH and exchangeable potassium (Kex).
The ring trial keeps the soils fixed and changes only the instrument. 60 of the soils come from KSSL, the largest part of OSSL. One of the instruments, the IAEA Thermo Nicolet, also measured the Fukushima soils of ossl-fuku-transfer. There the OSSL Kex model failed on the Fukushima spectra, and it is not settled whether the instrument or the soils caused it. If the model works on the IAEA spectra of these soils, the instrument is not the main cause.
The audience is soil scientists who transfer spectral models between instruments, and the readers of ossl-fuku-transfer.

title: OSSL to ring trial transfer
text:
Design

Question: the ring trial keeps the soils fixed and changes only the instrument, so it isolates cross-calibration. The project tests whether a CNN pretrained on OSSL can give the same prediction for a soil on every instrument. Exchangeable K is the main property, because of its role in the remediation of soils after a nuclear accident, and because it has no direct absorption band. Clay is the control, with a direct signal and a known cause for its bias on KSSL.
Data: soilspecdata’s load_ringtrial returns one Spectra per instrument, with the wet chemistry of the 70 soils.
Pretraining: OSSL v1.2 without 38 KSSL samples that are ring-trial soils. Their OSSL spectra correlate with the KSSL instrument’s ring-trial spectra at 0.99999 or more, and their clay, pH and Kex values are identical. The remaining 22 KSSL soils and the 10 NAPT soils have no match in OSSL.
Model: soilspecdl’s default SpectralCNN, the same CNN as in ossl-fuku-transfer, so the results of the two projects compare directly.
Split: on each instrument, grouped k-fold cross-validation over all 70 soils, repeated with different fold assignments. Near-duplicate soils, such as RT_04, RT_05, RT_07, RT_13 and RT_15, stay in one fold. The paper’s Kennard-Stone split (50 calibration and 20 test soils) is not used: it is optimistic, and its test set has only 20 soils.
Scores: Lin’s CCC, the paper’s main metric, and R². Every method uses the same folds, so methods are compared soil by soil, with paired tests.
Experiments:

Zero-shot (02_zero_shot): the OSSL models on every instrument, with no adaptation. The comparison with the paper’s Cubist, MBL and PLSR transfer results is not done yet.
Instrument model (03_instrument_model): the difference between each instrument and KSSL, modelled with a few physical effects that all its soils share.
Sensitivity (04_sensitivity): how much the predictions change under each of these effects.
Augmentation (05_augment, 06_aug_pretrain): pretraining with random instrument effects applied to the OSSL spectra, then zero-shot scoring on every instrument.
Fine-tuning (07_finetune): fine-tuning on the soils of one instrument, and ridge regression on frozen block-4 features, from three pretrained models, against PLSR trained only on those soils. The PLSR preprocessing is that of mirzai: SNV, a first-derivative Savitzky-Golay filter and removal of the CO₂ band. It has run for K and clay on KSSL and IAEA. 08_recalibrate compares it with linear recalibration, AdaBN and a refit of the head. 09_all_labs applies these corrections, PLSR and fine-tuning to all 21 instruments, from the unaugmented models. 10_where_it_fails finds where the zero-shot K spread comes from, and why the pretrained features fail on some instruments. Growing numbers of training soils, and the comparison of the gains with the paper’s instrument clusters and spectral dissimilarity are not done yet.

Aim: to understand what changes in the CNN under augmentation and fine-tuning, not to rank the methods by one score.

title: OSSL to ring trial transfer
text:
Notebooks

00_data: loads the spectra and the instrument table, groups the near-duplicate soils, and lists the 38 ring-trial soils that are in OSSL.
01_pretrain: trains one CNN each for clay, pH and K on OSSL, without those 38 soils, on SNV spectra, with the training settings of ossl-fuku-transfer but 80 epochs instead of 20.
02_zero_shot: scores the three models on all 21 ring-trial instruments, with no adaptation.
03_instrument_model: models the difference between each instrument and KSSL with a few physical effects shared by all soils, such as a gain, a baseline and a wavenumber shift.
04_sensitivity: measures how much the predictions of the three models change when one physical instrument effect, such as a wavenumber shift or a broadening, is applied to OSSL spectra.
05_augment: applies random shift, stretch, broadening, contrast, gain and baseline to OSSL spectra during pretraining, one transform for each effect, and compares the clay and K models with and without them.
06_aug_pretrain: finds how many epochs the augmented clay and K models need, and scores the augmented models that fine-tuning will start from.
07_finetune: fine-tunes the clay and K models on the KSSL and IAEA soils from three starting models, and compares fine-tuning, ridge regression on frozen features, zero-shot and PLSR, against wet chemistry and against the KSSL prediction.
08_recalibrate: compares fine-tuning with cheaper corrections fitted on the same soils: a bias, or a slope and bias, on the zero-shot predictions, AdaBN, and a refit of the head.
09_all_labs: applies the corrections, PLSR and fine-tuning to all 21 instruments, for K and clay, from the unaugmented models.
10_where_it_fails: tests whether the spread of the zero-shot K predictions comes from the model, the scans or the soils, relates the failure of the pretrained clay features to each instrument’s soil-specific difference from KSSL, and compares the IAEA shift with that of the Fukushima scans.

title: Recalibration
text:
Results
K: fine-tuning is a linear recalibration. A slope and bias fitted on the zero-shot predictions gives R² 0.54 to 0.61 on KSSL and 0.34 to 0.44 on IAEA, against 0.60 to 0.63 and 0.39 to 0.51 for fine-tuning. It recovers 75% to 115% of the fine-tuning gain on KSSL and 97% to 98% on IAEA. In the paired tests it is not significantly worse than fine-tuning, except from the augmented 20 model (p = 0.006 on KSSL and 0.03 on IAEA). The squared correlation of the zero-shot predictions, 0.57 to 0.63 on KSSL and 0.38 to 0.47 on IAEA, is about the R² that fine-tuning reaches. So with these soils, fine-tuning does not rank the soils better than the pretrained model already does. It corrects the scale and the offset: - The zero-shot predictions are too spread out. The slope of the targets on the predictions is 0.56 to 0.66 on KSSL and 0.44 to 0.46 on IAEA, where a calibrated model has 1. - On IAEA they are also too high, by 0.33 to 0.42 on the log1p scale. On KSSL the offset is only 0.01 to 0.05.
The lower ceiling on IAEA, with r² 0.38 to 0.47 against 0.57 to 0.63, is the part of the K problem that comes from the IAEA spectra. PLSR trained on IAEA reaches no more (0.40).
Clay: fine-tuning re-weights the features. A slope and bias recovers only 53% to 66% of the fine-tuning gain on KSSL and is significantly worse than fine-tuning in two of three cases (p = 0.005 and 0.009). On IAEA it reaches R² 0.21 to 0.47 against 0.69 to 0.73 (p ≤ 0.002). Refitting the head on the pooled features does much better: R² 0.90 to 0.94 on KSSL, matching or beating fine-tuning, and 0.58 to 0.70 on IAEA. From the unaugmented model on KSSL it beats fine-tuning (0.94 against 0.90, p = 0.047). On IAEA, fine-tuning still beats the head refit from two of the three starting models (p = 0.003 and 0.009). So the pooled features of the pretrained clay models carry what is needed on KSSL, and mostly on IAEA, but the OSSL head combines them in a way that does not suit these instruments. On IAEA, part of the gain needs changes inside the backbone.
AdaBN does not help. Recomputing the BatchNorm statistics on 63 soils removes part of the IAEA offset without targets, but a bias correction does better. AdaBN lowers zero-shot R² in 4 of the 12 cases, down to -0.51 for IAEA clay from the augmented 20 model. Once a slope and bias are fitted, AdaBN lowers R² in 10 of the 12 cases and raises it by at most 0.004.
The two properties therefore need different things. For K, the pretrained model sets the ranking, and the soils of an instrument only serve to calibrate it. A few soils with a linear correction may be enough, and better K needs better features, not more fine-tuning. For clay, the soils of an instrument re-weight the features, and on IAEA they also change the backbone.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from fastcore.test import *
from soilspecdl.all import SpectralCNN, regression_scores
from soilspecdata.datasets.ringtrial import load_ringtrial
from ossl_rt_transfer.data import rt_path, near_dup_groups
from ossl_rt_transfer.pretrain import model_dir, load_pretrained
The cells that read the ring-trial data and train are marked #| rtdata. The outputs on this page come from a local run.
This notebook tests what the pretrained CNNs gain from the soils of one instrument. On each instrument, the soils are split into grouped folds, and each method is trained on the other folds and predicts the held-out fold:
The CNN methods start from three pretrained models: the augmented 160-epoch models of 06_aug_pretrain, the augmented 20-epoch models of 05_augment, and the unaugmented 80-epoch models of 01_pretrain. This first run covers K, the main property, and clay, the control, on two instruments: KSSL, where pretraining has no instrument gap, and IAEA, the instrument of the Fukushima scans and the farthest from KSSL.

title: Fine-tuning
text:
Data and folds
rt_xy gives the spectra of one instrument after SNV, with the targets on the scale the models use: log1p for K. Every method gets these spectra. A second SNV, as in BatchSNV and in the PLSR pipeline, leaves them unchanged:



rt_xy
def rt_xy(
    spectra, # `Spectra` of one ring-trial instrument
    prop, # Ring-trial property, a key of `ossl_props`
)->tuple: # SNV spectra, targets (`log1p` for the properties in `log_props`), sample ids
Spectra and targets of the soils of one instrument that have a value of prop, on the scale the models use


soil_folds deals the near-duplicate groups of 00_data into folds. The folds are set by sample id, so a soil is in the same fold on every instrument, and the predictions of two instruments can be compared soil by soil:



soil_folds
def soil_folds(
    groups:pandas.Series, # Near-duplicate group of each soil, indexed by sample id
    k:int=10, # Number of folds
    repeats:int=10, # Number of fold assignments
)->pandas.DataFrame: # Fold of each soil, one row per repeat, one column per sample id
Grouped k-fold assignments, the same for a soil on every instrument



g = pd.Series([0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 5], index=[f'RT_{i}' for i in range(8)])
f = soil_folds(g, k=3, repeats=4)
test_eq(f.shape, (4, 8))
test_eq((f['RT_0'] == f['RT_1']).all(), True)
test_eq(f.loc[2, ['RT_6', 'RT_7']].nunique(), 1)

title: Fine-tuning
text:
Methods
plsr follows the PLSR pipeline of mirzai: SNV, a Savitzky-Golay first derivative with a window of 11 points and a polynomial of degree 1, and removal of the CO₂ region. fit_plsr chooses the number of components by grouped cross-validation on the training soils. finetune fine-tunes all of a copy of the pretrained model. The held-out soils are its validation set, so the loss, R² and bias on them are recorded after every epoch, but they play no part in training. ridge_block4 fits ridge regression on the frozen block-4 features, with the penalty chosen by leave-one-out cross-validation:



ridge_block4
def ridge_block4(
    model, # Pretrained `SpectralCNN`
    X, # SNV spectra on `rt_wns`, one per row
    y, # Targets
    train, # Indices of the training soils
    test, # Indices of the soils to predict
)->numpy.ndarray: # Predictions for `test`
Ridge regression on the frozen block-4 features of model, every channel at every position





finetune
def finetune(
    model, # Pretrained model
    X, # SNV spectra on `rt_wns`, one per row
    y, # Targets
    train, # Indices of the training soils
    test, # Indices of the held-out soils, only scored
    epochs, # Number of one-cycle epochs
    lr:float=0.003, # Maximum learning rate
    bs:int=16, # Batch size
    seed:int=0, # Seed for the training
)->tuple: # Predictions for `test`, and the held-out loss, R² and bias after each epoch
Fine-tune a copy of all of model on the soils train





fit_plsr
def fit_plsr(
    X, # Spectra on `rt_wns`, one per row
    y, # Targets
    groups, # Near-duplicate group of each soil
    max_components:int=15, # Largest number of components to try
    k:int=5, # Number of inner folds
):
plsr with the number of components that grouped inner cross-validation chooses





plsr
def plsr(
    n_components:int=10, # Number of PLS components
):
PLSR with the preprocessing of mirzai: SNV, Savitzky-Golay first derivative, CO₂ region removed


On random spectra and targets, each method returns one prediction per held-out soil, and finetune one row of history per epoch:

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Xs = preprocess().fit_transform(rng.uniform(0.2, 2, (40, len(rt_wns))))
ys, gs = rng.normal(size=40), np.arange(40) // 2
tr, te = np.arange(30), np.arange(30, 40)
test_eq(fit_plsr(Xs[tr], ys[tr], gs[tr], max_components=3).predict(Xs[te]).shape, (10,))
p, h = finetune(SpectralCNN(), Xs, ys, tr, te, epochs=2)
test_eq(p.shape, (10,))
test_eq(h.columns.tolist(), ['epoch', 'train_loss', 'valid_loss', 'r2', 'bias'])
test_eq(len(h), 2)
test_eq(ridge_block4(SpectralCNN(), Xs, ys, tr, te).shape, (10,))

choose_epochs cross-validates finetune over several numbers of epochs. cv_cnn and cv_plsr give the held-out predictions of every fold of every repeat, one row per soil:



cv_plsr
def cv_plsr(
    X, # Spectra on `rt_wns`, one per row
    y, # Targets
    ids, # Sample id of each row
    groups:pandas.Series, # Near-duplicate group of each soil, indexed by sample id
    folds, # Fold of each soil, from `soil_folds`
)->pandas.DataFrame: # Held-out predictions
Held-out predictions of fit_plsr, for every fold of every repeat





cv_cnn
def cv_cnn(
    model, # Pretrained model
    X, # SNV spectra on `rt_wns`, one per row
    y, # Targets
    ids, # Sample id of each row
    folds, # Fold of each soil, from `soil_folds`
    epochs, # Number of fine-tuning epochs
)->tuple: # Held-out predictions, and the fine-tuning histories
Held-out predictions of the pretrained model as it is, the block-4 ridge and the fine-tuned model, for every fold of every repeat





choose_epochs
def choose_epochs(
    model, # Pretrained model
    X, # SNV spectra on `rt_wns`, one per row
    y, # Targets
    groups, # Near-duplicate group of each soil
    grid:tuple=(10, 30, 100, 200), # Numbers of epochs to try
    k:int=5, # Number of folds
)->pandas.Series: # Mean held-out loss at the last epoch, for each number of epochs
Grouped cross-validation of finetune over the numbers of epochs in grid



ids = np.array([f'RT_{i}' for i in range(40)])
fs = soil_folds(pd.Series(gs, index=ids), k=4, repeats=2)
pc, hc = cv_cnn(SpectralCNN(), Xs, ys, ids, fs, epochs=1)
test_eq(len(pc), 3 * 2 * 40)
test_eq(pc.groupby(['method', 'repeat']).sample_id.nunique().unique(), [40])
test_eq(len(cv_plsr(Xs, ys, ids, pd.Series(gs, index=ids), fs)), 2 * 40)

paired_test compares two methods on the same units, such as soils or groups of near-duplicate soils. It takes the error of each method on each unit and applies a Wilcoxon signed-rank test to the differences:



paired_test
def paired_test(
    a:pandas.Series, # Error of method A on each unit, such as the mean squared error of a group of soils
    b:pandas.Series, # Error of method B on the same units
)->dict: # Number of units, mean error of A and B, share of units where A has the smaller error, Wilcoxon p-value
Wilcoxon signed-rank test of paired errors of two methods



e = pd.Series(rng.uniform(size=30))
r = paired_test(e, e + 0.1)
test_eq((r['n'], r['A_better']), (30, 1.))
assert r['p'] < 1e-3
test_eq(paired_test(e, e[::-1].reset_index(drop=True))['n'], 30)

cached saves each result table as a CSV file, so a rerun of a notebook loads it instead of computing it again:



cached
def cached(
    fname, # File name, without the `.csv` suffix
    f, # Function that computes the DataFrame
    path:NoneType=None, # Folder of the file, by default `finetune` in `model_dir()`
)->pandas.DataFrame: # The saved DataFrame, or the result of `f`
Load the DataFrame saved under fname, or compute it with f and save it



import tempfile
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    df = cached('t', lambda: pd.DataFrame({'a': [1, 2]}), d)
    test_eq(cached('t', lambda: None, d), df)

repeat_scores scores each repeat for each group of rows, pooling the held-out predictions of its folds. R² and CCC are on the scale the models use; RMSE and bias are on the property’s own scale. group_errors averages the squared error on the model scale over the repeats and over the soils of each near-duplicate group, the unit of paired_test:



group_errors
def group_errors(
    preds:pandas.DataFrame, # Held-out predictions, with columns `sample_id`, `y` and `pred`
    groups:pandas.Series, # Near-duplicate group of each soil, indexed by sample id
    keys:tuple=('instrument', 'property', 'start', 'method'), # Columns that define a group of rows
)->pandas.Series: # Mean squared error, indexed by `keys` and `group`
Mean squared error on the model scale of each near-duplicate group, over its soils and the repeats





repeat_scores
def repeat_scores(
    preds:pandas.DataFrame, # Held-out predictions, with columns `property`, `repeat`, `y` and `pred`
    keys:tuple=('instrument', 'property', 'start', 'method'), # Columns that define a group of rows
)->pandas.DataFrame: # Scores of `regression_scores`, one row per group and repeat
Scores of each repeat for each group of keys, each repeat pooling the held-out predictions of its folds



tp = pd.DataFrame({'instrument': 'A', 'property': 'potassium_cmolkg', 'start': 's', 'method': 'm', 'repeat': np.repeat([0, 1], 4),
                   'sample_id': ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'] * 2, 'y': [0., 1, 2, 3] * 2, 'pred': [0., 1, 2, 3] * 2})
test_eq(repeat_scores(tp)['R²'].tolist(), [1., 1.])
test_eq(group_errors(tp, pd.Series([0, 0, 1, 1], index=list('abcd'))).tolist(), [0., 0.])

title: Fine-tuning
text:
Number of epochs
On 63 training soils with a batch size of 16, an epoch is 3 or 4 optimiser steps. The ossl-fuku-transfer schedule of 20 epochs was chosen on about 1,000 samples and does not carry over. The number of epochs is chosen once for each property and starting model, by grouped 5-fold cross-validation over the KSSL soils, from 10, 30, 100 and 200 epochs. The same number then applies to every fold, repeat and instrument. Every KSSL soil is a test soil in some fold of the main run, so this choice uses soils that the main run later tests. It is one number out of four, so the optimism this adds is small. The table gives the mean held-out loss at the last epoch:

def epoch_table(p):
    X, y, ids = rt_xy(rt['KSSL'], p)

Cross-validation
Each instrument, property and starting model runs 10 grouped folds, repeated 10 times with different fold assignments. The predictions and fine-tuning histories are saved in res_dir, so a rerun of the notebook loads them:

title: Fine-tuning
Fine-tuning
text:
Results
Scores against wet chemistry. On KSSL, fine-tuning gives the highest R² for both properties and every starting model: 0.87 to 0.91 for clay and 0.60 to 0.63 for K. PLSR trained on the same soils gives 0.81 for clay and 0.15 for K. Zero-shot gives 0.68 to 0.76 for clay and 0.21 to 0.45 for K. For K, ridge regression on block-4 features (0.24 to 0.30) is below zero-shot from the augmented 160 model (0.45). CCC mostly agrees with R². The exception is K on KSSL: zero-shot CCC (0.73 to 0.78) is as high as fine-tuning CCC (0.77), although zero-shot R² is much lower (0.21 to 0.45 against 0.60 to 0.63).
On IAEA, fine-tuning and block-4 ridge give R² 0.60 to 0.73 for clay, against 0.45 for PLSR. For K, all methods except zero-shot give 0.38 to 0.51, and PLSR gives 0.40. Zero-shot on IAEA fails for K with every starting model: R² −2.1 to −3.3, with a bias of +0.66 to +0.87 cmol/kg.
IAEA stays below KSSL with every method, including PLSR trained on the IAEA spectra (clay 0.45 against 0.81). Part of the gap therefore seems to come from the IAEA spectra themselves, not from transfer.
Paired tests against PLSR. Fine-tuning and block-4 ridge beat PLSR on most soil groups for K on KSSL (71% to 86% of groups, p ≤ 0.001) and for clay on IAEA (68% to 81%, p ≤ 0.007). For clay on KSSL, fine-tuning lowers the mean squared error of PLSR by a third to a half, but has the smaller error on only 52% to 56% of groups (p = 0.06 to 0.46): the gain comes from a few soils. For K on IAEA, only fine-tuning from the augmented 20 model and block-4 ridge from the augmented 160 model beat PLSR at p < 0.05 (70% of groups, p = 0.02 and 0.03). With about 60 uncorrected tests, a few results at p < 0.05 are expected by chance.
Starting models. Augmentation improves zero-shot on IAEA clay: R² changes from −2.73 to 0.27 (augmented 160) and 0.40 (augmented 20), and the augmented models have the smaller error on about 90% of groups (p < 0.001). On KSSL clay, the augmented models are worse zero-shot (p = 0.01 and 0.02). After fine-tuning, the clay difference between starting models is not significant on either instrument (p = 0.20 to 0.64). For K, the augmented 160 model is worse than the unaugmented model after fine-tuning, on KSSL and on IAEA (smaller error on 22% and 29% of groups, p = 0.002 for both). The augmented 20 model is not significantly different (p = 0.19 and 0.68). The cost for K therefore goes with the long augmented pretraining, not with augmentation itself. Each starting model is one pretraining run with seed 42, so these differences include the variation between seeds.
Distance from the KSSL prediction. Fine-tuning and block-4 ridge bring the IAEA and KSSL predictions of a soil much closer than zero-shot does: 3.9 to 6.0% clay against 9.9 to 25.7% for zero-shot, and 0.10 to 0.13 against about 0.40 for K on the log1p scale. PLSR is further apart than fine-tuning for clay (7.0%) and similar for K (0.12).

title: Instrument model
text:
The model
For each soil, the KSSL spectrum is the reference. The model turns it into the spectrum that another instrument records for the same soil, with parameters shared by all soils of that instrument. The effects, applied in this order to raw absorbance:

shift: a wavenumber shift and stretch, applied by linear interpolation.
broaden: a Gaussian filter, for a coarser resolution.
contrast: absorbance raised to a power γ.
gain: multiplication by a smooth curve.
baseline: addition of a smooth curve.

Gain and baseline are B-splines with 10 basis functions over the whole range.

title: Instrument model
text:
Fitting
fit_instrument fits one model to the paired spectra of an instrument and KSSL. The loss compares the SNV of the modelled spectra with the SNV of the measured ones. SNV removes the offset and scale of each scan, so the model needs no parameters for single soils, and the error is on the scale the CNN sees. The CO₂ band is left out. Linear interpolation makes the loss uneven in the shift. A fit that starts from no shift can stop in a local minimum: for IAEA, at a shift of -1.5 cm⁻¹ instead of -2.5 cm⁻¹. When the model has a shift, fit_instrument starts it at each value in starts_cm and keeps the fit with the lowest loss.

Shared and soil-specific differences
Each model adds effects to the one above it. total is the RMS of the SNV residuals. shared is the RMS of their mean over soils: the part a model with shared parameters can remove. soil_specific is what remains after the mean is removed. For comparison, the spread between soils of the KSSL SNV spectra is 0.26.

The cells that read OSSL and the ring-trial data are marked #| rtdata. The outputs on this page come from a local run.
An augmentation engine for pretraining has to cover the instrument effects that the OSSL models react to most. This notebook applies each effect of InstrumentModel alone to OSSL validation spectra, at magnitudes that real instruments can have, and measures how much the predictions of the 80-epoch models of 01_pretrain change. Two measured differences give a scale: the difference spectrum D between the KSSL ring-trial spectra and the OSSL spectra of the same soils, and the effects fitted for MSU, IAEA and OSU in 03_instrument_model.

title: Sensitivity to instrument effects
text:
Effects in physical units
InstrumentModel sets its shift in points and its filter width as a logarithm, which suits fitting. perturb sets the same effects in physical units, and applies only the effects whose arguments differ from their defaults:



perturb
def perturb(
    X, # Absorbance spectra on `rt_wns`, one per row
    shift_cm:float=0.0, # Displacement of every band, in cm⁻¹, positive towards higher wavenumbers
    stretch:float=0.0, # Displacement of each band as a fraction of its wavenumber
    sigma_cm:float=0.0, # Standard deviation of a Gaussian broadening filter, in cm⁻¹
    gamma:float=1.0, # Contrast: absorbance raised to this power
    gain:NoneType=None, # B-spline coefficients added to a gain of 1, as in `InstrumentModel`
    baseline:NoneType=None, # B-spline coefficients of an additive baseline, in absorbance
)->numpy.ndarray: # Perturbed spectra
Apply the effects of InstrumentModel to X, with parameters in physical units


A band at 2000 cm⁻¹ moves 2 cm⁻¹ higher with a shift of 2 cm⁻¹, or with a stretch of 0.001. A Gaussian filter with σ = 6 cm⁻¹ widens a band of σ = 10 cm⁻¹ from a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 23.5 cm⁻¹ to √(10² + 6²) × 2.355 = 27.5 cm⁻¹. Counting the points above half the maximum, 2 cm⁻¹ apart, gives 22 and 26 cm⁻¹:

wn = rt_wns.astype(float)
band = np.exp(-0.5*((wn - 2000)/10)**2)[None]
peak = lambda x: wn[x.argmax()]
fwhm = lambda x: (x[0] > x.max()/2).sum()*2
test_eq(peak(perturb(band, shift_cm=2)), 2002)
test_eq(peak(perturb(band, stretch=1e-3)), 2002)
fwhm(band), fwhm(perturb(band, sigma_cm=6))

(np.int64(22), np.int64(26))

)->pandas.DataFrame: # One row per case
Mean and RMS of the change in the predictions of model when each function in cases is applied to X

section: A soil-specific part shared by the labs
text:
A soil-specific part shared by the labs
In 03_instrument_model, the first component of the soil-specific residuals lies on the quartz bands, and its scores correlate with clay with the same sign in 14 of the 20 labs. Part of the soil-specific difference may therefore be common to the labs: a difference between each soil’s KSSL spectrum and its spectrum in any other lab. For each instrument, the mean SNV residual of each soil over the other 19 instruments estimates this part without using the instrument’s own residuals. It is added to the SNV of the gain and baseline output. The table gives, over the 20 instruments, the correlation of each modelled change with the measured change, and their mean absolute difference:

snv = lambda X: (X - X.mean(1, keepdims=True))/X.std(1, keepdims=True)

resid = {i: pd.DataFrame(snv(paired[i][1]) - snv(gb_out(i)), index=paired[i][0]) for i in others}

    return pd.concat({p: sensitivity(models[p], Xr, cases).bias for p in ossl_props}, axis=1).unstack()

title: Sensitivity to instrument effects
text:
Consequences for augmentation

The models react most to a wavenumber shift or stretch, at sizes that real instruments have. An augmentation engine needs both, with shifts of at least ±2 cm⁻¹, the size fitted for IAEA.
Broadening to 8 cm⁻¹ and contrast within the fitted range change the predictions by about half the validation RMSE.
Smooth gain and baseline curves change the predictions least for their size.
The models react strongly to narrow features such as those of D, which smooth gain and baseline cannot produce.
On the ring-trial soils, the shared effects fitted for each instrument raise the clay predictions on 18 of the 20 instruments, while the measured spectra lower them on 14. For K, both raise the predictions on most instruments.
A soil-specific difference common to the labs explains about a third of the clay gap. Augmentation can add such terms at random for each scan, such as the quartz-band and water components of 03_instrument_model.
This check does not show whether augmentation makes the models stable on the measured spectra. Pretraining with augmentation, then scoring on the ring trial, is the test of that.

04_sensitivity showed that the OSSL models change their predictions under instrument effects of a size that real instruments have, most for clay and most for a shift of the bands to lower wavenumbers. This notebook applies the same effects at random to OSSL spectra during pretraining, so that the model sees each soil as different instruments would measure it. It then tests whether the augmented models transfer better to the ring-trial instruments.
Each effect is a separate fastai transform, so that any subset can go in the tfm list of pretrain, in any order. The transforms act on absorbance, before BatchSNV, and only on training batches.

title: Instrument augmentation
text:
Conclusions

The augmented models are 3 to 6 times less sensitive to shift, stretch and broadening, and half as sensitive to contrast. They lose about 0.01 in OSSL validation R².
Zero-shot R² on the ring trial improves for both properties and both seeds, by 0.05 to 0.09 for clay and by 0.17 to 0.20 for K. The variation between seeds is of the same size.
Predictions from the other instruments move only 5% to 10% closer to those from KSSL. Most of the gap between instruments is therefore not the effects that InstrumentModel describes.
